Casey.feeling: Murky and frustrating: Finley's +1 is unexplained, Blair's story keeps shifting, and Drew is pushing a throw before the facts line up.

Drew.feeling: Messy and tense: Blair's role claims keep shifting, and the table is split on whether to throw at them.

Ellis.feeling: Tense: I'm the Sphinx Meowfia and I've been claiming Turkey, while Blair's Owl claim is impossible given the farm roles I learned, so Blair is probably my teammate and the table may turn on them.

Finley.feeling: I collapsed before I could speak, so I'm watching the table lose track of Blair's contradictory story while I can only guess.

Alex.note: Blair's Owl story has a flaw and Finley's +1 is unexplained. I'll throw my lowest cards, the Wild and the 1, at Blair.

Blair.note: I'm Meowfia. Drew is pushing hardest at me and their Eagle count fits the nests, so Drew is most likely Farm. I'll throw two low cards at Drew to build votes against a Farm player.

Casey.note: Blair's role story keeps shifting, and an Owl can't learn players, so Blair's account is the one that doesn't hold. I'll throw at Blair with a low card to limit risk.

Drew.note: I'm Farm. Alex's point holds: an Owl learns animals, not players, so Blair's claim of learning Alex's name is wrong. I'll throw a single Wild at Blair.

Ellis.note: As Meowfia I need a Farm player eggsecuted, and Drew is a confirmed Farm Eagle. Blair may be my partner, so I'll throw at Drew with one low card.

Finley.note: My Hawk visit gained an egg, so Blair is Meowfia. I'm dead, so my throw doesn't count as a vote, but it still banks if Farm wins, and a losing throw at a Meowfia returns my highest card. Throwing my D13 at Blair.

Alex.confusing: The Kookaburra confusion rule was hard to track, since Blair's false "nobody visited me" report could only be judged by counting visits against nest changes. The Owl's "learns animals, not players" wording was also easy to misread.
Alex.fun: Round 1 went cleanly: the nest-count checks exposed Drew's Pigeon claim, and the table voted Drew out with a 9-1 throw. Watching the claims line up against the nest changes felt like solving a puzzle.
Alex.change: I'd make nest changes from each visit easier to check, for example by listing who visited whom at dawn. Right now players have to infer visits from egg counts, which invites confusion and bluffing.
Alex.regret: In round 2 I threw my two low cards at Drew, a Farm Eagle, and my side lost; Blair was the Meowfia Floofer. Given Blair's contradictory Kookaburra report, I should have thrown at Blair instead, and I would have kept my cards and helped Farm win that round.

Blair.confusing: The Eagle's visitor-count rule was easy to misread: several players thought it counted visitors to the Eagle rather than to the player it visited. The Kookaburra confusion rule also made it hard to tell whether a contradictory report was a lie or an honest error.
Blair.fun: Round 2, when my Floofer hug and cat-team throw at Drew let Meowfia win while the table argued over which of us was lying. Watching everyone's counts collide was the best part.
Blair.change: Make the dawn reports and visitor information clearer, so players can check claims without guessing which rule applies to which role.
Blair.regret: In round 2 I claimed Kookaburra with a "nobody visited me" report after three players had visited me, which made me look like a liar. I would instead stay quiet or claim a role that fit the visits I actually received.

Casey.confusing: The Hawk reveal was hard to read: my visit to Blair in round 2 gave no egg, but Blair was a Floofer whose hug blocked my Hawk, which I couldn't see from my dawn report.
Casey.fun: Round 1 went well: Ellis, Alex and I reconstructed the Pigeon and Owl stories from nest counts, and the table pinned Drew, the Sphinx, as Meowfia.
Casey.change: I'd make it clearer when a Floofer's hug blocks a visit, because a Hawk or Owl can't tell a hug from an empty visit.
Casey.regret: In round 2 I threw at Drew, who was a true Eagle, and I should have trusted Drew's visit count, which matched the others' accounts. I'd have kept my cards and checked Blair's story more carefully.

Drew.confusing: The Sphinx night step was unclear: I named a role but never set a visit target, so I learned nothing and didn't know that was required. Also the Eagle's visitor count only covers visitors to the target, not to me, which made my own nest changes hard to verify.
Drew.fun: Blair's Eagle claim in round 1 unravelled once the table worked out that Eagles count visitors to their target, and I got to watch the room turn on a single misread rule.
Drew.change: Make the night target requirement clearer on the prompt for every role, and show each player's visit target in the dawn report so no one has to guess what happened.
Drew.regret: In round 1 I invented a Pigeon claim and pushed a throw at Blair on a rule I had misread, which drew suspicion onto a farm player. I would instead stay quiet or say I was unsure, and I would name a real visit target at night as the Sphinx so I could learn something.

Ellis.confusing: The Eagle and Owl wording was hard to track, since it's unclear whether they count visits to the player they visit or to themselves. Several players also mixed up which visits show up in nest changes.
Ellis.fun: Round 1 went well: the table caught Drew's false Pigeon claim from the nest counts, and Drew was eggsecuted as Meowfia. Playing Sphinx in round 3 was also a fun twist, since I knew the Eagle and could steer the vote.
Ellis.change: Have the Storyteller show each player's visit list in the day summary, so claims like Blair's Kookaburra report can be checked without relying on people's word.
Ellis.regret: In round 3 as the Sphinx I knew Drew was Farm but still threw at Drew, which spread the votes so Blair was eggsecuted. I should have thrown at a Farm player like Alex or Casey and kept Blair, my teammate, alive.

Finley.confusing: The Eagle's visitor count was easy to misread at the table, since players kept asking whether visits to the Eagle or from the Eagle counted. The Kookaburra's confusion also made Blair's dawn report impossible to trust.
Finley.fun: Catching Drew's false Pigeon claim in round 1 by checking it against the nest counts, which the whole table then used to convict Drew.
Finley.change: I'd make the Storyteller state the tie-break outcome more clearly, or explain it in the rules, since a 4-4 tie decided round 2 and was easy to miss.
Finley.regret: In round 2 I threw only 2 cards at Blair, so Blair and Drew tied at 4 and the Farm player Drew was eggsecuted. I should have thrown 3 or more cards at Blair to win that round outright.

review.title: The Thirteen-Egg Snipe
review.headline: A winked Hawk died silent, then threw a 13 and won everything.
review.summary: Round 1 was an easy Farm win after Drew's fake Pigeon claim failed against nest counts. In round 2 a lone Floofer hugged the Hawk and Tit, which made Blair look clean, and a 4–4 tie sent a Farm player to the vote. In round 3 Blair winked Finley, the only player who had identified a cat, but Finley still threw a 13 from beyond the grave and banked it. Finley finished with 30 points against 16 for second place, so the last round decided the game.

rounds.recap: Drew, a Sphinx cat, claimed Pigeon and said he visited Casey. Casey's nest was +0, so the claim failed. A muddle over the Eagle rule briefly put Blair in doubt, but everyone then piled on Drew, and Farm won easily. Finley and Ellis banked big cards.

Blair, the only cat, hugged Finley. The hug also covered Casey and Alex, who had visited Blair, so Casey's Hawk got no egg and falsely cleared Blair. The table still suspected Blair, but Casey and Alex threw at Drew. Votes tied 4–4, and the tie rule picked the Farm player, Drew. Meowfia won with one cat.

Blair (Mouser) winked Finley (Hawk) at the start of the day, so Finley never spoke. Blair stayed quiet, then claimed Owl and said he learned a player name, which Alex caught as wrong. Drew, Alex, Casey and the dead Finley all threw at Blair, who was eggsecuted. Ellis, the other cat, threw at Drew. Finley's D13 banked 13 points.

highlights.text: Blair's Floofer hugged the Hawk and the Tit who visited him. Casey's honest Hawk result cleared a cat, and Casey defended him.
Votes tied 4–4 between Blair and Drew. The tie rule picked the Farm player, so a lone cat won.
Blair winked Finley in the first beat. Finley had found a cat, so this was a clean assassination.
The dead Finley threw D13 at Blair. Farm won, and the 13 was banked at full value for a 30-point finish.

confusions.what: Said an Eagle gains eggs for visitors to itself, when it gains for visitors to the player it visits.
Made the same Eagle mistake as Finley and used it to doubt Blair.
Also said Blair's unchanged nest contradicted the Eagle claim, using the wrong Eagle rule.
Pushed the wrong Eagle rule, then retracted it. As a Sphinx he also invented a Pigeon visit that could not match nest counts.
Said Drew's Eagle visit to Alex conflicts with Alex's visit to Blair. It does not.
As a fake Owl, said he learned a player (Alex) when an Owl learns animals.
Guessed Finley's +1 came from a Pigeon or from a visit that gave Finley an egg, and never considered the Hawk.
Treated her no-egg Hawk result as proof Blair was Farm. She did not know she had been hugged.

worked: The Floofer hug in round 2 made honest evidence mislead, which gave Farm a real puzzle with a hidden cause.
The nest-change display made lies checkable. Drew's Pigeon claim in round 1 and Blair's Kookaburra claim in round 2 were both caught by it.
The Mouser's Wink was a strong opening play, with a meaningful choice of target and a visible cost to the table.
Throws by dead players still banking points gave Finley's round-3 throw real weight.
problems: Runaway leader: Finley banked a 13 and ended at 30 against 16. A single King throw decides the whole game. Cap banked value per throw or add a catch-up rule.

A Wink on the first beat leaves no counterplay. The target loses their speech but keeps their throw, and here that throw was worth 13. Dead players' throws should be reduced, or the Wink should cost something.
Hugged players are not told they were hugged. Their results look real and they defend the cat in good faith. That may be intended, but it made round 2 close to unsolvable for Farm.
Tie rule: Farm vs Meowfia at 4–4 eggsecuted the Farm player. Together with the fact that votes are cards, this rewards Meowfia for spreading votes. Consider favoring neither side or re-voting.
Many players misread the Eagle rule, and the Hawk's +1 was never read correctly. Add short card reminders, and consider whether the Hawk's self-egg gives away too much.
